usage: 결과 + noun: the result OF something; the modifier comes first, no 의 needed
the verb of 'being released' is 나오다 with 이/가, never 를
attaches to a past-tense verb stem: 노력한 결과 = as a result of having tried
sentence-initial discourse connector linking a cause sentence to its outcome
examples: 시험 결과가 어때요?
How are your exam results?
Simple: 결과 as a plain noun taking 이/가 — note Korean has no plural -s
검사 결과가 아직 안 나와서 기다리고 있어요.
The test results haven't come out yet, so I'm waiting.
Everyday: the fixed collocation 결과가 나오다 for results being released
일 년 동안 열심히 운동한 결과 몸무게가 십 킬로그램이나 줄었어요.
As a result of exercising hard for a year, my weight dropped by a full 10 kg.
Real situation: -(으)ㄴ 결과 turns the whole first clause into the cause of the second
nuance: 결과 (結果, literally '結 form/bear + 果 fruit', i.e. the fruit that an action bears) is the end outcome of an action or event, and it almost always pairs with 나오다 (come out) or 나타나다 (appear) rather than any verb of 'making'. Its built-in partner is 과정 (the process leading up to it) and its mirror image is 원인 (the cause behind it), so Koreans constantly say 과정도 중요하고 결과도 중요하다. Register is neutral — fine in a doctor's office (검사 결과), a classroom (시험 결과), or a news report. The big English-speaker trap is twofold: first, you do not 'get' a result with a transitive verb the way English does — the result 나오다 (comes out) on its own and takes 이/가, so 결과를 나오다 is wrong; second, do not confuse the outcome 결과 with the reason 원인/이유 — 결과 is what happened at the end, never why.

mistakes: Don't say 결과를 나오다 — 나오다 ('come out') is intransitive, so the result takes 이/가: 결과가 나오다.
결과 is the outcome, not the cause; for 'the reason/cause' use 원인 (objective cause) or 이유 (personal reason), e.g. 사고의 원인, not 사고의 결과, when you mean what triggered it.
Don't force an English plural — there is no 결과들 in 'exam results'; 시험 결과 already covers singular and plural.

usage: 원인 names the objective, usually negative, source of a problem; 의 links the two nouns
the investigative collocation; also 원인을 밝히다 = uncover/clarify the cause
X이/가 원인이 되다 = X causes/leads to; subject takes 이/가, not 을/를
habitually modified by 근본적(인) 'fundamental' when discussing deep causes
examples: 감기의 원인이 뭐예요?
What's the cause of a cold?
Simple: 원인 as a plain noun with 의 joining it to 감기
스트레스가 여러 질병의 원인이 될 수 있어요.
Stress can become the cause of various illnesses.
Everyday: the X이/가 원인이 되다 pattern, where the cause is the subject
화재의 정확한 원인은 경찰이 아직 조사하고 있어요.
The police are still investigating the exact cause of the fire.
Real situation: 원인 with 조사하다/밝히다 in a serious, investigative register
nuance: 원인 (原因, '原 origin + 因 reason/factor', the originating factor) is the objective, analytical cause of a result — typically a problem, accident, illness, or phenomenon — and it locks together with 결과 as the textbook 원인과 결과 (cause and effect). The crucial dividing line for English speakers is 원인 vs 이유: 이유 is the personal reason or justification a person gives ('the reason I was late'), something you 말하다/대다 (state/offer), whereas 원인 is an impersonal cause you 찾다/밝히다/조사하다 (find/uncover/investigate). So '왜 늦었어요?' is answered with an 이유, never an 원인. Register is neutral-to-formal, common in news, medicine, and engineering. Watch the particle: the cause is the subject of 되다, so it is 원인이 되다, and you say 'X가 Y의 원인이다' (X is the cause of Y), not the reverse.

Say 원인이 되다 ('becomes a cause'), not 원인을 되다 — 되다 takes 이/가 on the thing it turns into.
Don't reverse the of-relation: 'the cause of the accident' is 사고의 원인, not 원인의 사고.

usage: fixed phrase on immigration/visa forms; also 방문 목적 = purpose of visit
the right verb is 이루다 (accomplish) or 달성하다, never 하다
describes an intended aim behind an action; 뚜렷한 목적이 있다 = have a clear aim
Verb-는 것이 목적이다 states what the aim is
examples: 이번 모임의 목적이 뭐예요?
What's the purpose of this gathering?
Simple: asking for the aim of an event with 의 + 목적
이 프로그램의 목적은 외국인을 돕는 것이에요.
The purpose of this program is to help foreigners.
Everyday: the N의 목적은 -는 것이다 framing that defines a purpose
친구가 모임 목적이 뭐냐고 물어봐서 '그냥 같이 밥 먹는 거'라고 대답했어요.
My friend asked what the purpose of the gathering was, so I answered 'just to eat together'.
방문 목적, 여행 목적 — '~ 목적' asks the aim/reason
nuance: 목적 (目的, '目 eye + 的 target' — the target your eye is fixed on) is the conscious aim or intention behind an action, more deliberate and goal-directed than 이유 (the reason behind it) or 원인 (the cause that produced it). Compare the near-synonym 목표: 목표 is a concrete, often measurable target you aim to hit (this month's sales 목표, a finish-line 목표), while 목적 is the underlying purpose or 'what it is for' — a company's 목적 may be 'to help people' but its 목표 is 'sell 1000 units'. Register leans formal/written: it dominates immigration forms (방문 목적), reports, and mission statements. Two pitfalls: do not pair it with 하다 (you 이루다/달성하다 a 목적, you never 목적을 하다), and do not confuse 목적 (purpose) with 목적지 (目的地, 'purpose-place' — the destination, an actual place).

Use 이루다/달성하다 with 목적, not 하다: 목적을 이루다 ('achieve a purpose'), never 목적을 하다.
Don't use 목적 where 목표 fits: a numeric/concrete target ('my goal is to lose 5 kg') is 목표, while 목적 is the broader 'what it is for'.

usage: 과정 follows a noun to name a developmental process over time
Verb-는 과정에서 = while/during the process of; highlights events along the way
the dedicated verb is 거치다 (pass through stages), not 가다
also a formal program: 박사 과정 = a doctoral program
examples: 요리하는 과정이 재미있어요.
The cooking process is fun.
Simple: -는 과정 nominalizing 'the process of cooking'
한국어를 배우는 과정에서 실수를 많이 했어요.
I made a lot of mistakes in the course of learning Korean.
Everyday: -는 과정에서 framing events that happen along the way
이 신청은 서류 심사, 면접, 최종 발표까지 여러 과정을 거쳐야 해요.
This application has to go through several stages: document screening, an interview, and the final announcement.
Real situation: 과정을 거치다 listing concrete bureaucratic stages
nuance: 과정 (過程, '過 pass through + 程 a stage/measured stretch') is the unfolding process — the sequence of stages something passes through over time — and it also doubles as a formal 'course' of study (교육 과정, 박사 과정, 정규 과정). Its natural opposite is 결과 (the final outcome), which is why Koreans pair them: 결과보다 과정이 중요하다. A close relative is 절차, but 절차 is the fixed set of official procedures/steps you must follow (a legal 절차, an application 절차), while 과정 is the broader, more organic course of how things actually develop. The standout pattern is -는 과정에서 'in the course of doing', perfect for describing side-events that occur while a bigger thing happens. Pitfalls: use 거치다 (not 가다) for 'go through stages', and beware the homophone-ish 과장 (誇張 exaggeration, or 課長 a section chief) — a single jamo separates them.

usage: very common compound (人間關係) for one's web of social ties; written as one word
관계가 좋다/나쁘다 describes the quality of a relationship; subject takes 이/가
이웃과의 관계 = relationship with neighbors; 와/과 marks the other party
be related, have to do with
X와/과 관계가 있다 = is connected to X; 관계없다 = irrelevant
examples: 친구와의 관계가 좋아요.
I have a good relationship with my friend.
Simple: N과의 관계 + 좋다 for relationship quality
그 일은 저와 아무 관계가 없어요.
That matter has nothing to do with me.
Everyday: 관계가 없다 = unrelated, also 'none of my business'
이번 사건은 그 회사의 자금 문제와 깊은 관계가 있는 것으로 보여요.
This incident appears to be deeply connected to that company's financial troubles.
Real situation: abstract 관계가 있다 linking two facts/events in a formal report tone
nuance: 관계 (關係, '關 a barrier-gate that connects + 係 to tie/link' — a binding link) spans two senses: warm personal relationships (인간관계, 친구 관계, 부부 관계) and abstract relations or connections between facts, events, or ideas. With 있다/없다 it shifts toward 'to be related / have to do with', so 관계없다 / 관계가 없다 is the everyday way to say 'irrelevant' or 'none of my business' (relevant-but-blunter than English). Mark the other party with 와/과, and note the formal genitive 와/과의 관계. A near-synonym is 사이 ('the space between' two people), which is more colloquial and intimate — 우리 사이 좋아 ('we're close') feels warmer and chattier than 우리 관계 좋아, which sounds more analytical. The classic English-speaker slips: never say 관계를 있다 (it must be 관계가 있다), and do not confuse 관계 (relationship) with the look-alike 관심 (關心, interest/attention).

Don't mix up 관심 (interest, 'I'm interested in K-pop' = K팝에 관심이 있다) with 관계 (relationship); they share 관 but mean different things.
For casual closeness between friends, 사이 is often more natural than 관계: 우리 사이 좋아 sounds warmer than 우리 관계 좋아.

usage: X이/가 Y에/에게 영향을 주다 = X affects Y; everyday register
X에게서/에서 영향을 받다 = to be affected by X; the receiving side
more formal than 주다; standard in writing and news
modified by 좋은/나쁜/큰 to describe the effect's quality and size
examples: 날씨가 기분에 영향을 줘요.
The weather affects my mood.
Simple: N에 영향을 주다 — the affected target takes 에, not 을/를
저는 어릴 때 할머니께 많은 영향을 받았어요.
I was greatly influenced by my grandmother when I was little.
Everyday: 영향을 받다 with 께 for the respected person who influenced you
이번 정책은 자영업자들에게 큰 영향을 미칠 것으로 보입니다.
This policy is expected to have a big impact on the self-employed.
Real situation: formal 영향을 미치다 in news/report register
nuance: 영향 (影響, '影 shadow + 響 echo' — a shadow-and-echo that one thing casts onto another) is influence or impact, and it crucially works in two opposite directions you must keep straight: the source 영향을 주다 / 미치다 (gives/exerts an effect) while the recipient 영향을 받다 (receives/is affected). 미치다 is the formal, news-and-essay verb for 'exert an effect', whereas 주다 is everyday conversation. The decisive English-speaker trap is the particle: the affected target is marked with 에 (for things — 환경에 영향을 주다) or 에게/께 (for people — 아이들에게/부모님께 영향을 주다), NOT with 을/를, because the actual object slot is already filled by 영향(을). So 'it affects the environment' is 환경에 영향을 줘요, never 환경을 영향을 줘요. Compare 효과 (效果, the resulting effect/efficacy of a measure, e.g. 약의 효과 'the medicine's effect'): 영향 is the act of influencing, 효과 is the beneficial result that comes out.

Don't use 영향 for the beneficial 'effect' of a remedy — that is 효과 (약의 효과); 영향 is the broader, often neutral act of influencing.

usage: 상황 follows a noun/modifier naming the state of affairs
상황이 좋다/나쁘다/심각하다 describe how things stand; subject takes 이/가
frames advice or a reaction to a set of conditions
상황에 따라(서) 다르다 = it depends on the situation
examples: 지금 상황이 어때요?
How's the situation right now?
Simple: 상황 with 이/가 asking after the state of things
이런 상황에서는 어떻게 해야 할지 모르겠어요.
In a situation like this, I don't know what I should do.
Everyday: 이런 상황에서(는) framing a reaction to circumstances
회사 사정이 어려워서, 상황에 따라 채용 일정이 바뀔 수도 있어요.
Since the company is in a tough spot, the hiring schedule may change depending on the situation.
Real situation: the hedging phrase 상황에 따라 in a workplace context
nuance: 상황 (狀況, '狀 condition/form + 況 circumstances' — the configuration of circumstances) describes the overall set of conditions surrounding a moment or event, broader than a single 경우 (a specific case or instance — 이런 경우 = 'in this one case', vs 이런 상황 = 'in this whole situation'). The reflexive phrase 상황에 따라(서) 다르다 ('it depends on the situation') is one of the most useful hedges in Korean, and 이런/그런 상황에서 sets up advice or reactions. Register is neutral. Two pitfalls: keep 상황 (the circumstances around an event) distinct from 상태 (狀態, the state/condition of a single thing or body — 건강 상태 'health condition', 배터리 상태 'battery state'); you describe a person's mood with a 상태, but the events around them with a 상황. And use 에 따라 (not 으로) for 'depending on': 상황에 따라, never 상황으로.

Use 에 따라 for 'depending on the situation', not 으로: 상황에 따라(서), never 상황으로.
For one specific instance, 경우 is sharper than 상황: '이런 경우' = 'in this particular case' vs '이런 상황' = 'in this whole situation'.

usage: common for job/contract terms; 조건이 좋다/나쁘다 rates the deal
갖추다 = to be equipped with / fulfill; also 조건을 만족하다
조건 follows a noun naming the relevant terms (계약 조건 = contract terms)
조건에 맞는 사람 = a person who fits the requirements; 에 맞다, not 을 맞다
examples: 이 일은 조건이 좋아요.
This job has good terms.
Simple: 조건이 좋다 rating an offer's terms
지원하려면 몇 가지 조건을 갖춰야 해요.
To apply, you have to meet a few requirements.
Everyday: 조건을 갖추다 = fulfill the requirements
월급은 마음에 드는데 근무 조건이 안 맞아서 고민이에요.
I like the salary, but the working conditions don't suit me, so I'm torn.
Real situation: 근무 조건 weighed in a realistic job-decision context
nuance: 조건 (條件, '條 an article/clause + 件 an item' — itemized clauses) means both the requirements that must be satisfied and the terms/conditions of an arrangement (jobs, contracts, deals, even relationships). With 갖추다/만족하다 it means 'fulfill requirements'; with 맞다 it means 'fit/match the conditions'; and a great everyday word is 조건이 좋다 ('the terms are good'). It is more concrete than 상황 (the overall circumstances): 조건 are the specific, often listed terms, not the general state of affairs. The number-one English-speaker trap is grammatical interference: 'if' in the sense of a conditional sentence is the verb ending -(으)면, NOT the noun 조건. You cannot say '조건 you come, ...' — say '오면 ...'. Use 조건 only as the noun 'a condition/requirement'. Also note 조건에 맞다 (fit) takes 에, while 조건을 갖추다 (possess/fulfill) takes 을.

usage: 기준이 높다/낮다/엄격하다 describe how strict a standard is
based on / using N as the standard
성적을 기준으로 = on the basis of grades; do not drop 으로
기준에 맞추다 = to align/adjust to the standard
기준 follows a noun naming what the standard is for (채용 기준 = hiring criteria)
examples: 기준이 너무 높아요.
The standard is too high.
Simple: 기준이 높다 describing a strict benchmark
나이를 기준으로 줄을 섰어요.
We lined up based on age.
Everyday: N을/를 기준으로 = using N as the reference point
이 제품은 정부의 안전 기준을 모두 통과했습니다.
This product passed all the government's safety standards.
Real situation: 안전 기준 + 통과하다 in an official/regulatory register
nuance: 기준 (基準, '基 foundation + 準 a level/measuring standard' — a foundational measuring line) is the standard or yardstick against which things are measured, judged, or sorted. The workhorse phrase N을/를 기준으로(하다) means 'taking N as the basis/reference point' and is everywhere when explaining how something is organized or decided (나이를 기준으로, 가격을 기준으로). The key contrast is 기준 vs 조건: 기준 is the measuring criterion itself (the bar you measure against), while 조건 is a requirement that must be met — a job's 채용 기준 (hiring criteria, the yardstick) differ from its 지원 조건 (application requirements you must satisfy). Register is neutral-to-formal, heavy in administration, hiring, and regulations. Pitfalls: never drop the 으로 in the set phrase (it is N을 기준으로, not N을 기준), and mind the vowel — 기준 (standard) is not 기분 (氣分, mood/feeling).

usage: to some degree, roughly how much
어느 정도 알아요 = I know to some extent; also asks 'how much, roughly?'
그 정도면 충분해요 = that much is enough
한 시간 정도 = about an hour; attaches after a quantity
울 정도로 = to the point of crying; shows intensity
examples: 한 시간 정도 걸려요.
It takes about an hour.
Simple: N 정도 after a quantity = 'approximately'
한국어를 어느 정도 할 수 있어요.
I can speak Korean to some degree.
Everyday: the set phrase 어느 정도 = 'to some extent'
어제는 말도 못 할 정도로 피곤해서 일찍 잤어요.
Yesterday I was tired to the point I couldn't even speak, so I slept early.
Real situation: -(으)ㄹ 정도로 conveying how extreme the state was
nuance: 정도 (程度, '程 a stage/measure + 度 a degree' — a measured degree) expresses degree or extent, and after a number it means 'about/approximately', overlapping with 쯤 but slightly broader: 쯤 attaches tightly to points in time/space (세 시쯤 'around 3'), while 정도 also covers amounts and intensity (열 명 정도 'about ten people', 그 정도 'that much'). The set phrases 어느 정도 ('to some extent') and 그 정도 ('that much') are essential intermediate vocabulary, and the grammar -(으)ㄹ 정도로 ('to the extent/point that') is the go-to way to dramatize how strong something is (죽을 정도로 'to death'). Register is fully neutral. The main English-speaker trap is redundancy: because 정도 already means 'about', do not also add 약 ('approximately') — 약 한 시간 정도 doubles up; pick one, normally 한 시간 정도. Also keep 정도 (degree/extent) apart from the look-alike 제도 (制度, a system/institution).

usage: the natural intransitive way to say a change arises; subject takes 이/가
분위기에 변화를 주다 = add a change to the mood/atmosphere
modified by 급격한/큰/작은 to describe scale and speed
the thing you adapt to takes 에: 변화에 적응하다
examples: 요즘 날씨 변화가 심해요.
These days the weather changes a lot.
Simple: 변화가 심하다 = the change is severe/big
기분 전환하려고 머리 스타일에 변화를 줬어요.
I changed up my hairstyle for a change of mood.
Everyday: 변화를 주다 = deliberately introduce a change for variety
새로운 환경의 변화에 적응하는 데 거의 반년이 걸렸어요.
It took nearly half a year to adapt to the changes of the new environment.
Real situation: 변화에 적응하다 over a realistic adjustment period
nuance: 변화 (變化, '變 to alter + 化 to transform' — alteration-and-transformation) is the noun 'change', used for shifts in states, trends, weather, society, technology, or one's life, and it is more abstract and global than the plain verb 변하다/바뀌다 (a specific thing changes). Distinguish 변화를 주다 ('introduce/make a change', usually for freshness or variety) from 변화가 생기다 ('a change occurs' on its own), and mark what you adapt to with 에 (변화에 적응하다). The subtle English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 변화하다 as the verb for everyday change: 변화하다 exists but sounds formal/scientific ('the climate is changing' 기후가 변화하다), so for ordinary 'something changed' use 변하다 or 바뀌다 (전화번호가 바뀌었어요 'my number changed'), and reserve 변화 for the noun. Compare 발전 (發展, development/progress — change specifically in a better, advancing direction), which carries positive growth that neutral 변화 does not.

usage: 의미 있는 일 = a meaningful thing; covers both 'significant' and 'has a meaning'
the everyday way to say something has no point
축하하는 의미에서 = in the spirit of celebrating
결과에 의미를 두다 = to attach significance to the result
examples: 이 단어는 무슨 의미예요?
What does this word mean?
Simple: asking a word's meaning — though casual speech often prefers 뜻
감사하는 의미에서 작은 선물을 준비했어요.
I prepared a small gift as a token of thanks.
Everyday: -는 의미에서 = 'in the sense/spirit of'
혼자 떠난 여행은 저에게 특별한 의미가 있었어요.
The trip I took alone had a special significance for me.
Real situation: 의미가 있다 in the deeper 'significance/value' sense
nuance: 의미 (意味, '意 intention/thought + 味 flavor' — the flavor of an intention) covers both the literal 'meaning' of a word and the deeper 'significance/value' of an experience, so 의미가 있다 elegantly straddles 'has a meaning' and 'is meaningful'. Its near-synonym 뜻 overlaps heavily but skews toward literal word-meaning and is the more colloquial choice: when asking 'what does this mean?' in everyday speech Koreans usually say 무슨 뜻이에요?, saving 의미 for writing or for talking about significance (큰 의미가 있다). The pattern -는 의미에서 ('in the sense/spirit of doing') is a handy intermediate connector for spelling out the intention behind an action. Register is neutral; 뜻 just feels a notch warmer and more spoken. Pitfalls: say 의미가 있다, never 의미를 있다; and don't assume 의미 and 뜻 are always interchangeable — 뜻 also means 'one's will/intention' (그 뜻을 따르다 'follow that wish'), a sense 의미 lacks.

usage: 중요한 역할을 하다 = to play an important role; also for the function of a thing
맡다 = to be put in charge of a role/part; stresses being assigned
modified by 중요한/큰/핵심적인 to rate its weight
splitting up who does what within a team
examples: 각자 역할이 있어요.
Each person has their own role.
Simple: 역할이 있다 = to have a role; 각자 = each person
선생님은 학생들에게 중요한 역할을 해요.
Teachers play an important role for students.
Everyday: 역할을 하다 = play/serve a role
이번 연극에서 저는 주인공 역할을 맡게 되었어요.
In this play I ended up taking on the lead role.
Real situation: 역할을 맡다 for being cast/assigned a part
nuance: 역할 (役割, '役 a duty/service + 割 a portion' — the portion of duty allotted to you) is the role or part a person, factor, or even an object plays, covering family members (가족 안에서의 역할), team assignments, and the function of things or causes. 역할을 하다 means 'to play/serve a role', while 역할을 맡다 emphasizes being assigned or taking the part on (맡다 = be put in charge). Pronunciation is a real trap: 역할 is pronounced [여칼], with the final ㄱ aspirating the following ㅎ, so learners who say [역할] sound off; and the single most common native misspelling is 역활 — even Koreans get it wrong, but the standard form is 역할. A near-synonym is 기능 (機能, function), but 기능 is the mechanical/technical function of a system or device (이 버튼의 기능 'this button's function'), while 역할 implies a part played within a larger whole, often by a person. Use 맡다 (not 잡다) for taking on a role.
